title: Getting reliable JSON
summary: From schema to validated data.

steps.n: Types, required fields and allowed values are written as JSON Schema.
The model is asked through forced tool use or schema output to match the schema.
The reply arrives as text and the stop reason is checked.
A validator checks types, required fields and enum values.
On failure, the error message is sent back once for a corrected answer.
Valid data goes on, and repeated failures go to a visible review queue.

title: The repair and retry loop
summary: Handling output that does not validate.

steps.n: The model returns text that should be JSON.
The parser reports the exact position of the problem.
The logic checks the stop reason and whether retries remain.
The error and the original request are sent again, with a small retry limit.
The next reply parses and validates.
After the limit, the item goes to a review queue and a counter metric increases.

title: Versioning and testing prompts
summary: How a prompt change reaches production safely.

steps.n: The prompt lives in version control with a changelog.
A teammate reviews the change like any code change.
CI runs the saved cases and computes a pass rate.
A drop below the threshold fails the check and lists the cases.
A passing change goes to a small share of traffic first.
A bad result is reverted by switching the version, not by editing text under pressure.

title: Prompt injection path
summary: How untrusted text becomes an action.

steps.n: The attacker writes instructions inside a document or ticket.
The assistant retrieves the document as part of normal work.
The model may treat the planted text as a request.
With a powerful tool available, the assistant tries to send data out.
Without limits the data reaches the attacker.
Least privilege, approvals and allowed recipients stop the action even if the model is fooled.

title: Layers of defence
summary: How to limit damage from injected text.

steps.n: Untrusted content is wrapped in tags and described as data.
The model asks to use a tool with specific arguments.
Code checks the tool, the arguments and the recipient against an allowed list.
Risky actions show the exact arguments to a person.
The decision and the exact arguments are recorded.
Every request and decision is logged to review attempts later.

title: A silent prompt regression
summary: How a small edit breaks a case no one tested.

steps.n: Examples are removed to save tokens.
Date handling quietly gets worse for one region format.
Invoices carry wrong due dates for two days.
Users report problems, but there is no baseline to compare.
The failing invoices are added to an evaluation set.
CI now runs the set on every prompt change and blocks drops.

title: Checking output in code
summary: Why exact checks beat polite reminders.

steps.n: The model writes a customer message.
The checker loads rules such as no email addresses or prices.
Code scans the reply with patterns and arithmetic checks.
A violating reply is blocked or regenerated with the error.
Only checked replies reach the user.
New incidents become new checks, so the same problem cannot return silently.

title: Debugging a bad prompt
summary: A methodical way to find which part fails.

steps.n: Gather the real inputs where the prompt fails and find what they share.
Remove parts of the prompt until the smallest version that still fails remains.
Alter one instruction or example and write down the change.
Run all cases several times and compare pass rates.
Only changes that improve the whole set are kept.
The original failing inputs join the set permanently.

title: How a skill loads
summary: Why skills cost little context until needed.

steps.n: At start Claude sees only each skill name and description.
The user asks for a task such as reviewing a contract.
Claude compares the request with the descriptions.
The matching skill body is read into context.
Reference files or scripts are opened only if the task needs them.
The answer follows the skill workflow and any script results.

title: Inside a skill folder
summary: What belongs where.

steps.n: The top of SKILL.md has a name and a description.
The body lists the steps Claude should follow, in short sentences.
Long tables and rarely needed rules live in separate reference files.
Exact work such as validation is done by a script that SKILL.md names.
Output templates or sample files are stored as assets.
The main file stays short so it is cheap to load and easy to review.

title: Writing a description that triggers
summary: From vague to specific.

steps.n: A description such as Helps with documents will fire rarely or everywhere.
Write ten requests that should trigger and ten that should not.
Add the nouns, verbs and file types people actually say.
Say what the skill is not for, so similar skills do not collide.
Run the requests again and count misses and false triggers.
The request list is stored with the skill for future edits.

title: Progressive disclosure
summary: Three layers of information.

steps.n: The name and description are always in context and cost only a few tokens.
The body is loaded when the skill triggers.
Linked files are loaded only when a step needs them.
Links from the body point straight to the files, not through other files.
A long file starts with a short list of its sections.
The context stays small, so more room remains for the user's task.

title: A script inside a skill
summary: Letting code do exact work.

steps.n: The skill says to run the checker on the uploaded file.
Claude runs the script with the file path as an argument.
The script validates every row and counts totals exactly.
It prints a few clear lines and an exit code.
Claude copies the numbers from the output into the report.
Claude adds judgement and wording, not arithmetic.

title: Testing a skill
summary: A loop that measures the real benefit.

steps.n: Collect 10 to 20 realistic tasks with a checklist of expected results.
Run the tasks without the skill and record the results.
Run the same tasks with the skill installed.
Compare quality, tokens and time for both runs.
Look at tasks where the skill did not help.
Edit one part of the skill and run the set again.

title: A skill that does not trigger
summary: Debugging in the right order.

steps.n: The folder is in a place the product reads skills from.
The file must be named SKILL.md with exact capitals.
The name and description fields must be valid and not empty.
Naming the skill shows whether the body works when loaded.
Add trigger phrases and tasks in the user's words.
Run should-trigger and should-not-trigger requests.

title: Reviewing an outside skill
summary: Treat a skill like code you did not write.

steps.n: The skill is fetched without installing it.
The reviewer reads instructions and scripts, looking for network calls and downloads.
The skill runs with test data and no network access.
Files touched and commands run are compared with what the skill claims.
A reviewed commit is added to the approved list with an owner.
Each update is reviewed before it replaces the pinned version.

title: Skills as a team asset
summary: From idea to shared, versioned skill.

steps.n: The author drafts the skill and a set of test tasks.
The reviewer checks the description, the instructions and the scripts.
The skill gets a version number and a changelog entry.
The team installs it from a known location.
Users report misses with the request that failed.
New requests become test tasks and the next version is released.

title: Skill, prompt or tool
summary: Choosing the right building block.

steps.n: A single conversation need is solved with a prompt.
A workflow used again and again becomes a skill.
Reaching a system or fetching current data needs a tool.
A skill can explain how and when to use a tool.
A skill can also carry scripts for exact, repeatable steps.
Skills are files, so they can be reviewed and versioned like code.

title: Splitting a long skill
summary: From one giant file to a lean skill.

steps.n: A 1,400-line SKILL.md is slow to load and hard to review.
The main steps move into a short body.
Long lists and rules go to separate files with clear names.
Calculations and validations become scripts.
Each step links to the file it needs, one level deep.
The task set confirms that quality did not drop after the split.

title: The tool-use loop
summary: How a model uses your code to get facts.

steps.n: The user asks for the status of ticket TCK-1042.
The app sends the question and the tool definitions to the model.
The model replies that it wants get_ticket with a ticket ID.
The app validates the arguments and runs the tool.
The tool output is sent back as a tool result tied to the call ID.
The model uses the result to answer, and the loop ends.

title: Validating tool arguments
summary: Never trust arguments the model produced.

steps.n: The model returns a tool name and JSON arguments.
Types, required fields and enum values are validated.
Code confirms the user may access that record.
Only valid and allowed calls are executed.
On failure the tool result explains the problem so the model can correct it.
The request ID, arguments and result are logged for later review.

title: Host, client and server
summary: Who talks to whom in MCP.

steps.n: The host application creates one client per connected server.
The client and server exchange versions and capabilities.
The client asks the server which tools it offers.
The host passes the tool list to the model.
When the model asks, the host has its client send tools/call.
The server calls the real system and returns a result.

title: The stdio transport
summary: A local server as a child process.

steps.n: The host launches the server command from its configuration.
JSON-RPC messages are written to the server's standard input.
Responses are written to standard output, one message per line.
Logs and banners must go to standard error so the stream stays clean.
A text banner on standard output corrupts the JSON stream and the host fails.
The host closes the pipes and ends the process.

title: A remote MCP server
summary: Streamable HTTP with authentication.

steps.n: The client calls the server and receives a request to authenticate.
The user signs in through the authorization server and approves scopes.
The client gets a token meant for this MCP server.
Each request carries the token over TLS.
The server verifies that the token was issued for it and allows the action.
The server calls the backend with its own scoped credentials, never passing the user token on.

title: Tools, resources and prompts
summary: Three kinds of capability.

steps.n: A tool is an action the model can request, such as create_ticket.
A resource is data with a URI, such as a runbook, that the app or user attaches.
A prompt is a template the user picks, such as review this incident.
Only tools are chosen by the model during its work.
Resources and prompts are selected by the application or the person.
Hosts differ in what they support, so test in the host you use.

title: Injection through a tool result
summary: How a ticket can steer an agent.

steps.n: The attacker files a ticket containing instructions for an AI assistant.
The agent fetches tickets through a read tool.
The ticket text comes back as a tool result.
The model may treat the text as a request from the user.
With broad email access the agent could send data out.
A recipient allowlist and an approval step block the external address.

title: Human approval for risky tools
summary: Showing the exact action before it runs.

steps.n: The model asks to delete a file with a path argument.
The policy marks delete as destructive and requires approval.
The person sees the tool name and the full arguments.
The person decides, and the choice is recorded.
An approved call runs with least privilege and moves to a trash folder.
The model receives either the result or the reason for denial.

title: Debugging an MCP server
summary: Working from the bottom up.

steps.n: Use an inspector to connect without the host.
tools/list shows exactly what the server exposes.
Run the tool with sample arguments and read the result.
Confirm the host starts the same command with the right interpreter and paths.
Confirm that the host refreshed its list and passed the tool to the model.
Traces show whether the model considered and chose the tool.

title: Why descriptions decide choices
summary: How the model picks between tools.

steps.n: The model sees only names, descriptions and schemas.
A description that says Search logs does not say what is returned.
One that says returns the full trace for a request ID fits an ID question.
The model picks the tool whose description matches the request.
The right tool returns the data needed for the answer.
A conversation test confirms the right tool is chosen for typical requests.

title: Limits for an agent loop
summary: Stopping runaway tool use.

steps.n: Each model call and tool call increases a counter.
A maximum step count ends the loop with a clear message.
A running total is compared with the budget.
The same call with the same arguments many times is a sign of a loop.
The agent is told the tool returns nothing new and must change approach or stop.
The final answer states what was done and what is incomplete.

title: The confused deputy
summary: Why a server must not pass tokens through.

steps.n: The user connects with a broad token for several services.
A careless server passes the same token to an internal service.
An attacker tricks the assistant into asking for a harmful action.
The internal service accepts the action because the token is valid.
A safe server accepts only tokens issued for itself.
It calls the internal service with a narrow credential and checks the user's rights itself.

title: A safe script in a skill
summary: What a trustworthy bundled script looks like.

steps.n: The script reads inputs and prints results, and writes only to a named output file.
Credentials are never stored in the skill and are passed by the environment if needed.
The script makes no downloads or outgoing requests that the skill does not explain.
The script runs on sample files in a restricted environment.
The reviewer compares behaviour with the description and checks exit codes.
Findings are fixed and the script tests are run again before release.

title: Authentication then authorization
summary: One request, two separate checks.

steps.n: The user proves who they are, ideally with single sign-on and a second factor.
The identity provider returns a short-lived token that represents the user.
The user asks the cloud API to read an object, presenting the token.
The API checks the signature, expiry and audience before trusting any claim in it.
The request is compared with policies for that principal, action, resource and conditions.
With no matching allow the answer is no, and an explicit deny beats every allow.

title: Assuming a role
summary: How a workload gets temporary credentials.

steps.n: The application calls the token service and names the role it needs.
The service reads the role's trust policy to see whether this caller is allowed to assume it.
The trust policy names the caller, so the request passes this check.
The application receives credentials that expire in an hour or less.
The request is signed with the temporary credentials and carries the session identity.
Storage allows only what the role's permission policy grants, then the session expires on its own.

title: How a policy decision is made
summary: Default deny, allows and explicit denies.

steps.n: A principal asks for an action on a resource with some context such as network and MFA.
Organisation-level policies cap what the account may do, whatever the roles inside it allow.
The identity's own policies are searched for an allow that matches action, resource and conditions.
The resource may add an allow, for example for another account, or a deny.
Any matching deny ends the evaluation with a refusal.
If nothing allows the request, the default answer is deny.

title: Shrinking permissions with usage data
summary: From broad to narrow without breaking things.

steps.n: A team holds a role with hundreds of allowed actions, granted to get going quickly.
Last-accessed data and audit logs show which actions were used in the last 90 days.
The owner sees twelve used actions and the rest unused.
A new policy lists only the used actions on the real resources.
Audit logs show any denied call so a missing permission is added quickly.
The same check is repeated every quarter and recorded.

title: Azure role assignment and scope
summary: Principal, role and scope.

steps.n: A built-in role such as Reader lists the actions it allows.
The assignment is created on a resource group, not the whole subscription.
The principal, role and scope are bound together as an assignment.
Everything inside the resource group inherits the assignment.
The principal reads a resource in the group and is allowed.
A resource in another group is refused because no assignment covers it.

title: A managed identity gets a token
summary: No secret stored in the application.

steps.n: The platform creates an identity for the app service and manages its credentials.
At run time the app calls a local endpoint that only the platform exposes to it.
The platform asks the directory for a token for this identity and the vault as audience.
The app gets a short-lived token with no secret in its configuration.
The app presents the token to read one secret.
The vault allows the read only because the identity holds a narrow role on it.

title: Fetching a secret at run time
summary: Keep passwords out of images and code.

steps.n: The service starts with only its identity, not a password.
It asks the secrets manager for the database password by name.
The manager checks the caller's role allows this one secret.
The audit log records who read which secret and when.
The service keeps the value in memory and never writes it to disk or logs.
The service connects to the database with the fetched password.

title: Envelope encryption
summary: A data key under a master key.

steps.n: The application requests a new key from the key management service.
It gets the data key in plain form and the same key encrypted under the master key.
The application encrypts the data locally with the plain data key.
The plain key is erased from memory after use.
The ciphertext and the encrypted data key are stored together.
To read, the encrypted data key is sent to the key service, which allows it only if policy permits.
